plain.en: not enough of something for everyone who wants it

means.en: Wants are more than the resources that can meet them. Scarcity forces people, firms and governments to choose.

plain.en: something we must have to live

means.en: Food, clean water, shelter and clothing are needs. Needs keep life possible.

plain.en: something we would like to have but can live without

means.en: A new phone or a video game is a want. Human wants are unlimited: when one is met, a new one comes.

plain.en: a choice about how to use limited money, time or other resources

means.en: People, enterprises and governments all make economic choices, for example a farmer choosing which crop to grow.

plain.en: any place where buyers and sellers meet

means.en: A market can be a shop, a weekly bazaar or an app on a phone.

plain.en: things we use to make goods and services

means.en: Natural resources include water and coal. Human-made resources include machines, capital and technology. Resources are limited and have many uses.

plain.en: the ground and everything nature gives, such as water, soil and minerals

means.en: Land is one of the factors of production.

plain.en: knowledge and methods for making things better or faster

means.en: Technology is one of the factors of production. Better technology can make more from the same resources.

plain.en: the study of how people make choices with limited resources

means.en: Economics studies how choices are made by making the best use of limited resources to meet needs and wants.

plain.en: all the producing, buying, selling and money flows of a country or region

means.en: The economy is the state of a country or region in terms of production, consumption and the flow of money.

plain.en: a person or firm that makes and sells goods or services

means.en: Producers pay wages to workers and sell goods to consumers.

plain.en: the way a country answers what to produce, how and for whom

means.en: The three economic systems are planned, market and mixed.

plain.en: how much buyers want to buy at a price

means.en: When demand rises and supply stays the same, the price usually rises.

plain.en: the work people do, with their hands and minds

means.en: Labour is one of the factors of production. Workers are paid wages for their labour.

plain.en: machines, tools, buildings and money used to produce goods

means.en: Capital is one of the factors of production. A sewing machine in a workshop is capital.

plain.en: the value of the next-best choice you give up

means.en: When you choose one thing, the best thing you could have had instead is its opportunity cost. It is not always money.

plain.en: a graph of all the best mixes of two goods that can be made with the resources we have

means.en: Each point on the curve is a full use of the land or workers. Points inside the curve leave some resources idle. Points outside cannot be reached.

plain.en: one possible mix of two things

means.en: On a farm, one combination might be 25 kg of barley and 90 kg of wheat.

plain.en: a business, such as a farm, a shop or a firm

means.en: Enterprises decide what to make, how much to make and how to make it.

plain.en: the four things used to produce goods: land, labour, capital and technology

means.en: Every good or service is made with some mix of the factors of production.

plain.en: not being used

means.en: Land or workers that are idle are not producing anything.

plain.en: the players in an economy

means.en: Consumers, producers, the government and financial institutions such as banks are the economic entities.

plain.en: a person who buys and uses goods and services

means.en: Consumers pay prices to producers.

plain.en: banks and similar bodies that keep money and give loans

means.en: Banks are financial institutions. They take deposits and give loans.

plain.en: money paid to a worker for work

means.en: A tailor earns a wage for each day of work.

plain.en: money people and firms pay to the government

means.en: The government uses taxes to pay for roads, schools, street lights and other public goods.

plain.en: facts and numbers collected for study

means.en: Good plans use data instead of guesswork.

plain.en: a planned way of collecting and studying facts

means.en: Economists use surveys to collect data, for example on how families spend money.

plain.en: a plan of action chosen by a government or a firm

means.en: Economists study data to help governments make good policies, such as on taxes or prices.

plain.en: a yearly report on the state of India's economy

means.en: The Ministry of Finance presents it in Parliament before the Union Budget.

plain.en: the government's yearly plan of how it will earn and spend money

means.en: The Union Budget is presented in Parliament every year.

plain.en: help for people who need it, such as food, pensions or health care

means.en: Governments run welfare programmes for people who are poor, old or ill.

plain.en: how much sellers have to sell at a price

means.en: Demand and supply together set prices in a market economy.

plain.en: the money a seller earns after paying all costs

means.en: The chance of profit leads firms to make what buyers want.

plain.en: using more workers and fewer machines

means.en: Farming and handicrafts are often labour-intensive.

plain.en: using more machines and fewer workers

means.en: Making steel and cars is capital-intensive.

plain.en: an economy where the government decides what to produce, how and for whom

means.en: In a planned economy, the government owns most factories and land and a planning office makes the decisions.

plain.en: an economy where private owners decide, guided by demand and supply

means.en: In a market economy, individuals and private companies own most factories, shops and land.

plain.en: an economy where the government and private firms both make economic choices

means.en: Almost all economies today are mixed. India is a mixed economy.

plain.en: sellers trying to win the same buyers

means.en: Competition pushes sellers towards better quality, lower prices and new ideas.

plain.en: goods everyone can use, which no seller can charge each user for

means.en: Roads, parks, street lights, police and basic education are public goods. The government provides them from taxes.

plain.en: official permission from the government to do something

means.en: Before 1991, many Indian firms needed licences from the government to make or expand goods.

plain.en: firms owned and run by the government

means.en: Railways and many banks in India are in the public sector.

plain.en: a business owned by private people, not the government

means.en: Private firms work for profit and compete with each other.

plain.en: big changes to rules to make things work better

means.en: In 1991, India made major economic reforms: fewer rules, more private enterprise and more trade with other countries.
